question: What are the characteristics of the main AC electrical supply?

options.text: 115 volt, 60 Hz, single phase
28 volt, 400 Hz, single phase
200 volt, 60 Hz, three phase
115 volt, 400 Hz, three phase

explanation: The high frequency allows lighter transformers and motors, which is why aircraft use 400 Hz rather than a commercial frequency.

question: How many engine driven generators are installed?

options.text: One, on the left engine only
Two, one on each engine
Three, including a standby generator
Four, two on each engine

explanation: One generator per engine, with the APU generator available as a third source, gives redundancy without added complexity.

question: What is the purpose of the drive unit in an integrated drive generator?

options.text: It holds the generator at constant speed so the output frequency stays constant
It steps the generator output up to 115 volts
It disconnects the generator automatically at high engine speed
It converts the generator output from DC to AC

explanation: Engine speed varies continuously in flight, so a mechanical drive is used to isolate the generator from those changes.

question: What is the approximate rating of each main generator?

options.text: 40 kVA
60 kVA
90 kVA
150 kVA

explanation: The rating determines what can be carried on a single generator after a failure. Verify against your operator FCOM.

question: Can two AC sources supply the same transfer bus at the same time?

options.text: Yes, but only on the ground
Yes, provided both are within frequency tolerance
No, the system is non parallel and only one source supplies a bus
Yes, whenever the bus transfer switch is in AUTO

explanation: Without paralleling there is no need to synchronise sources, and a fault on one source cannot be fed by another.

question: What happens on a transfer bus when its own engine generator is brought on line?

options.text: It shares the load with the previous source
It is blocked until the previous source is switched off manually
It powers only the galley loads until selected
It takes over the bus and disconnects the previous source

explanation: The engine generator has priority on its own side, so restoring it does not require the crew to remove the other source first.

question: Which source has priority when both the APU generator and external power are available?

options.text: Neither, the crew must select one manually
The APU generator
Whichever was connected first
External power

explanation: Selecting the APU generator automatically removes external power, which makes the transition to airplane power a single action.

question: Where is the external power receptacle located?

options.text: In the left wing root fairing
In the nose wheel well ceiling
In the aft fuselage near the APU
In the lower forward fuselage

explanation: Placing it forward keeps the cable clear of the engines and the loading areas during turnaround.

question: What does an illuminated blue ground power available light indicate?

options.text: External power is connected and within acceptable limits
The ground service bus is energised
External power is supplying the transfer buses
External power is connected but out of tolerance

explanation: The light confirms the quality of the supply, but the power is not on the airplane until it is selected.

question: What is the function of the bus tie breakers?

options.text: They allow one source to supply both transfer buses
They protect the generator against overvoltage
They connect the transformer rectifier units to the AC buses
They isolate the battery from the DC buses

explanation: The tie is what makes single source operation possible after the loss of a generator.

question: What is the effect of selecting the bus transfer switch to OFF?

options.text: Both transfer buses are de-energised
The standby system transfers to the battery
The APU generator is disconnected
Automatic bus tie operation is prevented, so a bus loss is not covered automatically

explanation: It is used to keep a faulty side isolated, at the price of losing the automatic transfer that would normally restore the bus.

question: What does a TRANSFER BUS OFF light indicate?

options.text: That transfer bus is not energised
The bus transfer switch is in the OFF position
The generator is running but not connected
The transformer rectifier on that side has failed

explanation: It reports the state of the bus itself, which is the information the crew needs before deciding which source to restore.

question: What does a GEN OFF BUS light indicate?

options.text: The generator drive has been disconnected
The generator has failed completely
The generator is operating but is not supplying a bus
The generator is supplying only the galley loads

explanation: It distinguishes an available but unconnected source from a source that is genuinely lost.

question: What does a SOURCE OFF light indicate?

options.text: The bus is not being supplied by its normal source
The generator control unit has failed
The battery is not charging
External power has been disconnected

explanation: It draws attention to a bus running on an alternative source, which matters because the load capacity may then be limited.

question: Which loads are shed first when electrical capacity becomes limited?

options.text: The fuel boost pumps
The window heat
The galley loads
The flight instruments

explanation: Galley equipment draws a large current and contributes nothing to safety, which makes it the natural first load to remove.

question: What typically causes automatic galley load shedding?

options.text: Selection of the bus transfer switch to OFF
Operation on a single generator or on a limited capacity source
Loss of one transformer rectifier unit
Engine anti-ice selection

explanation: With one source carrying the whole airplane the margin is reduced, so non essential load is removed automatically.

question: What is displayed by the AC meters on the electrical panel?

options.text: Transformer rectifier output only
Voltage, frequency and load for the selected source
Battery charge current only
The total DC load on the battery bus

explanation: Selecting each source in turn is how the crew verifies that a generator is producing acceptable power before connecting it.

question: Can the APU generator supply both transfer buses?

options.text: No, it supplies transfer bus 2 only
Yes
Only when external power is also connected
No, it supplies transfer bus 1 only

explanation: Full airplane coverage from the APU is what makes it usable as a complete substitute after a generator failure.

question: What limits the availability of APU electrical power in flight?

options.text: The position of the bus transfer switch
A maximum altitude for APU generator use
The cabin differential pressure
The number of engines operating

explanation: Both the APU and its generator have altitude related limits. Verify the figures against your operator FCOM.

question: What causes the amber DRIVE light to illuminate?

options.text: Low oil pressure or high oil temperature in the generator drive
Loss of generator output voltage
Disconnection of the generator from the bus
A frequency outside the acceptable range

explanation: The light reports the mechanical health of the drive, which can fail even while the generator is still producing acceptable power.

question: What is the crew action for a drive unit with low oil pressure?

options.text: Transfer the bus to the APU and continue with the drive connected
Reduce the electrical load on that side
Reset the generator control breaker
Disconnect the drive

explanation: Disconnecting protects the engine accessory gearbox from a seizure that would otherwise damage far more than the generator.

question: Can a disconnected generator drive be reconnected in flight?

options.text: Yes, but only with the engine at idle
Yes, by cycling the generator switch
No, reconnection requires maintenance action on the ground
Yes, after the drive has cooled for ten minutes

explanation: The decision to disconnect is effectively permanent for that flight, which is why it is taken deliberately and not as a trial.

question: Why should the generator drive not be disconnected while the engine is not running?

options.text: The battery would be discharged by the disconnect solenoid
The oil in the drive would drain into the engine
The generator control unit would be damaged by the voltage transient
The disconnect mechanism requires rotation to operate correctly

explanation: Attempting it at rest risks leaving the mechanism in a condition that requires more extensive maintenance to restore.

question: What is the immediate consequence of disconnecting a generator drive in flight?

options.text: That generator is unavailable for the remainder of the flight
The engine must be shut down
The other generator is also load shed
The battery assumes the entire AC load

explanation: Planning for the rest of the flight has to assume single generator operation, with the APU as the only remaining alternative.

question: How is an integrated drive generator cooled?

options.text: By engine fan air
By ram air ducted from the nacelle inlet
By fuel passing through a heat exchanger
By its own oil system

explanation: The same oil that lubricates the drive carries away the heat, which is why oil temperature is a direct indication of drive health.

question: What does the generator control unit protect against?

options.text: Overheating of the transfer bus wiring
Loss of oil pressure in the engine
Out of tolerance voltage and frequency conditions
Excessive engine vibration

explanation: Connecting a source producing bad power would damage equipment across the airplane, so the unit prevents the connection.

question: How many transformer rectifier units are installed?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

explanation: Three units allow each DC bus to have its own supply with one unit remaining as a backup for either side.

question: What does a transformer rectifier unit do?

options.text: It converts AC into DC
It changes the frequency of the AC supply
It converts DC into AC
It regulates the battery charging voltage

explanation: Most of the airplane DC load is supplied by conversion rather than by the battery, which is reserved as a last resort.

question: What is the role of the third transformer rectifier unit?

options.text: It supplies the standby DC bus at all times
It supplies the battery bus only
It is used only during engine start
It can supply either DC bus if one of the other units fails

explanation: Its flexibility is what allows a single unit failure to be covered without losing a DC bus.

question: What is the consequence of losing all AC generation for the DC system?

options.text: The transformer rectifier units stop and DC comes from the battery
DC is unaffected because it is generated separately
Only the standby DC bus is lost
The battery charger maintains the DC buses indefinitely

explanation: The DC system depends on AC being available, which is why a total generation failure quickly becomes a battery endurance problem.

question: What type of main battery is fitted?

options.text: A 48 volt nickel metal hydride battery
A 24 volt nickel cadmium battery
A 12 volt lead acid battery
A 28 volt lithium ion battery

explanation: Nickel cadmium construction tolerates the high discharge rates of an engine or APU start and a wide temperature range.

question: What is special about the hot battery bus?

options.text: It is supplied by the static inverter
It is powered only when the battery switch is ON
It is powered only on the ground
It is connected directly to the battery regardless of the battery switch position

explanation: Certain functions, including fire protection items, must be available even with every switch off.

question: What determines whether the switched hot battery bus is powered?

options.text: The availability of external power
The position of the standby power switch
Whether an engine is running
The position of the battery switch

explanation: It carries loads that should be available whenever the airplane is being operated, but not while it is parked and shut down.

question: What is the function of the battery charger?

options.text: It isolates the battery when the airplane is parked
It converts battery DC into AC for the standby bus
It limits the current drawn during engine start
It maintains the battery in a charged state from the AC system

explanation: Without it the battery would be progressively depleted by each start and by the standby loads.

question: What is the purpose of the static inverter?

options.text: It converts AC into DC for the battery bus
It converts battery DC into AC to supply the AC standby bus
It regulates the frequency of the generator output
It provides a starting current for the APU

explanation: Some essential equipment is AC only, so a source of AC has to exist even when no generator is turning.

question: What are the positions of the standby power switch?

options.text: AUTO, MAN and BAT
ON, OFF and TEST
NORM, ALTN and OFF
BAT, OFF and AUTO

explanation: AUTO is the normal selection, leaving the transfer to battery power to happen without crew action.

question: With the standby power switch in AUTO, what happens if normal power is lost?

options.text: The APU starts automatically
The standby buses transfer automatically to the battery and static inverter
The standby buses remain unpowered until BAT is selected
The standby buses are shed to preserve the battery

explanation: The automatic transfer means the essential instruments and radio are not interrupted while the crew diagnoses the failure.

question: What does the STANDBY PWR OFF light indicate?

options.text: The standby power switch is in AUTO
A standby bus is not powered
The battery is discharging
The static inverter is supplying the AC standby bus

explanation: Losing the standby buses means losing the last protected layer, so it is annunciated separately from the main bus lights.

question: Which of the following is typically supplied by the standby power system?

options.text: Essential flight instruments and one communication radio
Both packs and the recirculation fans
The autopilot and the autothrottle
The galley outlets and the cabin lighting

explanation: The selection is what a crew needs to fly, navigate and communicate, and nothing more.

question: For approximately how long can the battery support the standby loads?

options.text: About 5 minutes
About 30 to 60 minutes
About 3 hours
About 10 hours

explanation: The endurance sets the time available to reach an airport after a total generation failure. Verify the figure against your operator FCOM.

question: Why must the battery switch be ON before an engine start?

options.text: It energises the generator field
It powers the fuel boost pumps directly
It supplies the control and ignition circuits and protects the buses during the start
It provides the air pressure for the starter

explanation: The start sequence depends on DC control power, and the battery also stabilises the system through the electrical transients.

question: Why is the battery considered the final layer of the electrical system?

options.text: Because it has the largest capacity of all the sources
Because it can be recharged in flight indefinitely
Because it supplies every bus on the airplane
Because it produces power without depending on any other system

explanation: Every other source needs something else to be working, whereas the battery is self contained.

question: What is the purpose of the ground service switch?

options.text: It powers cabin lighting and service outlets from external power without energising the whole airplane
It isolates the galleys during refuelling
It transfers the standby buses to the battery
It connects external power to both transfer buses

explanation: Cleaners and caterers can work with the airplane otherwise unpowered, which saves both APU running and wear.

question: Where is the ground service switch normally located?

options.text: At the forward attendant station
On the aft electronic panel
At the external power receptacle
On the overhead panel

explanation: It is placed where the cabin crew or ground staff can reach it without entering the flight deck.

question: What happens to the electrical system when the second engine generator is brought on line after start?

options.text: Both generators parallel and share the load equally
The bus tie breakers open and isolate both buses
It takes its own transfer bus and the APU is relieved of that side
The APU generator is tripped off immediately

explanation: Each generator resuming its own side is what allows the APU to be shut down once both are on line.

question: What supplies the airplane electrically during an engine start when no generator is available?

options.text: The battery alone
The transformer rectifier units working in reverse
The static inverter
The APU generator or external power

explanation: The start requires both electrical control power and a bleed source, which is why the APU normally provides both.

question: What is the effect of losing one engine generator in flight with the bus transfer switch in AUTO?

options.text: The remaining source supplies both transfer buses through the bus ties
The affected bus transfers to the battery
The standby power system takes over both buses
Both transfer buses are lost until the APU is started

explanation: The automatic tie is what makes a single generator failure a largely transparent event for the crew.

question: Which system depends on AC power to deliver fuel to the engines under normal conditions?

options.text: The fuel boost pumps
The fuel temperature indication
The fuel crossfeed valve
The engine driven fuel pumps

explanation: The boost pumps are AC motors, which is why a total AC failure changes how the engines are fed.

question: Which ice protection load is electrical rather than pneumatic?

options.text: Engine cowl anti-ice
Wing anti-ice
Window and probe heating
Both wing and cowl anti-ice

explanation: Electrical heating is used where the area is small and the temperature must be closely controlled.

question: Why does the loss of AC power affect the flight instruments differently from the loss of DC power?

options.text: Because the flight instruments are all DC powered
Because the flight instruments are all AC powered
Because the instruments transfer to the FMC supply
Because the standby system provides both AC and DC to the essential instruments through different paths

explanation: Understanding which supply feeds which display is what allows the crew to predict what will remain after a given failure.

question: Where are the main circuit breaker panels located?

options.text: On the forward overhead panel
In the electronics bay only, accessible from outside
On the aft flight deck panels behind the pilot seats
On the centre pedestal

explanation: They are within reach in flight so that a tripped breaker can be identified, though resetting is restricted by procedure.

question: What is the general rule about resetting a tripped circuit breaker in flight?

options.text: Breakers are reset automatically by the system
It is not reset unless the associated system is essential and the reset is permitted by procedure
Breakers are reset only after landing
Any breaker may be reset once

explanation: A breaker trips because something drew excessive current, and restoring power to a fault can turn an electrical problem into a fire.

question: Why is a total loss of AC generation described as time limited?

options.text: Because the standby buses shed automatically after a fixed period
Because the transformer rectifier units overheat on battery power
Because the battery endurance determines how long the essential loads can be supplied
Because the static inverter has a limited operating time

explanation: The failure converts into an endurance problem, so the first decision is where the airplane can land within the available time.

question: What is the normal position of the bus transfer switch?

options.text: OFF, under a guard
AUTO, without a guard
AUTO, under a guard
OFF, without a guard

explanation: The guard keeps the system in the configuration that provides automatic protection, and makes any change a deliberate act.

question: Why are the flight deck electrical panel lights and indications checked before the first flight of the day?

options.text: To reset the battery charger cycle
To confirm that source availability and bus status can be correctly annunciated
To warm the generator control units before start
To discharge the static inverter

explanation: An annunciation that cannot illuminate is a failure the crew would never see, which is why the indications themselves are verified.

question: What is the relationship between the APU generator and the engine generators in flight?

options.text: The APU generator can supply only the standby buses in flight
The APU generator can be used only on the ground
The APU generator can replace either or both engine generators
The APU generator parallels with the engine generators to share the load

explanation: Its ability to substitute completely is what makes it valuable after a generator failure at altitude.

question: What does the crew verify before disconnecting external power after an APU start?

options.text: That the standby power switch is in BAT
That the APU generator is supplying the buses
That the battery switch is OFF
That the bus transfer switch is OFF

explanation: Confirming the replacement source is carrying the airplane prevents an unnecessary interruption to the buses.

question: What happens to the DC buses when their normal supply is lost?

options.text: They are shed until AC power is restored
They transfer to the static inverter
They are supplied from the remaining transformer rectifier unit or from the battery
They are supplied from the galley buses

explanation: The layering of sources means a DC bus is lost only after several independent failures.

question: Why is the electrical system designed so that no single failure removes all generation?

options.text: Because several systems needed for continued safe flight have no non electrical alternative
Because paralleled generators cannot be isolated
Because the APU cannot be started above its altitude limit
Because the battery cannot be recharged in flight

explanation: Instruments, displays, fuel delivery and much of the ice protection all depend on power, so generation redundancy is a flight safety requirement.

question: What does the current and potential selector on the electrical panel allow the crew to do?

options.text: Reset a tripped generator control breaker
Display the output of each electrical source in turn
Transfer the standby buses between sources
Select which source supplies each bus

explanation: It is a monitoring control rather than a switching control, used to check a source before or after it is connected.
